Certainly! Here’s a ghost story set in ancient China:

---

On the jade-lit banks of the Wei River, nestled among whispering bamboo and ancient willow, there once stood a scholar’s house. The learned Xu Wen was known across the provinces for his wisdom, but in the Year of the Black Tiger, his heart ached from solitude—his beloved wife, Mei, had passed away one autumn eve, her laughter now only a faint memory in the halls.

In the months after Mei’s death, Wen poured all his grief into poetry, often reciting verses late into the night. One moonless evening, as plum blossoms scattered across his courtyard, Wen heard a delicate knocking at his lattice door. He opened it to find a woman veiled in moon-pale silk. Her voice quavered like a flute, “My lord, I am cold, and lost. May I find shelter beside your lantern’s warmth?”

Moved by pity and curious dread, Wen led her inside. Her beauty shimmered with a ghostly light, and as she sat, her shadow did not touch the floor. She spoke in riddles, her words filled with longing. As midnight approached, she begged, “Pray, play the qin for me. Let me remember what it was to be alive.”

Wen played, and his song awoke a sorrow so deep that his eyes blurred with tears. As the final note faded, the stranger’s veil slipped—beneath, her face was Mei’s, serene and pale as paper, eyes brimming with unwept tears.

“Beloved,” Wen whispered, “why do you return in this form?”

Mei’s spirit replied, her voice lighter than wind, “The bonds of love and promise kept me wandering. Your mourning binds me to this world. Set me free, my husband; let your heart find peace, that I may find rest.”

The next dawn, Mei’s form melted into the dawn mist. Xu Wen, his grief eased, buried her favorite hairpin beneath the plum tree, and recited a poem of farewell. That night, for the first time in many moons, the old house was filled not with sorrow, but with the soft fragrance of plum blossoms, and the gentle laughter of a promise kept.

---

Thus, in the scrolls of the Wei River villages, it is said: spirits linger on sorrow, but love—when let go—can bring both the living and the dead to peace.
